blocks.text: In the popliteal fossa, the tibial nerve is positioned laterally to the popliteal artery and vein. As it continues its course, it crosses to the medial side of the popliteal artery, becoming more superficial as it descends.
**Tibial Nerve Origin and Course:** The tibial nerve, a major branch of the sciatic nerve, originates from the ventral branches of the fourth and fifth lumbar and first to third sacral rami.
It travels down the back of the thigh, enters the popliteal fossa, and passes anterior to the soleus arch, continuing into the leg.
In the popliteal fossa, it becomes superficial and is lateral to the popliteal vessels, eventually crossing to the medial side of the popliteal artery. (Option A, B & D ruled out)
In the leg, it descends with the posterior tibial vessels, lying on the tibialis posterior and bifurcating under the flexor retinaculum into the medial and lateral plantar nerves.
Branches:

items.text: **Articular Branches:** Supply the knee joint.
**Muscular Branches:** Innervate gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, popliteus, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, and flexor hallucis longus.
**Sural Nerve:** Descends between gastrocnemius heads, supplying the posterior and lateral skin of the distal leg and foot.
**Medial and Lateral Plantar Nerves:** Innervate the muscles and skin of the sole.
**Medial Calcaneal Nerve:** Supplies sensation to the heel area.

blocks.text: **Tibial Nerve Clinical Significance:** The tibial nerve is prone to injury in the popliteal fossa and can be compressed at the tendinous arch of the soleus, leading to potential damage from compartment syndrome or tarsal tunnel syndrome.

The ligaments of the hip joint are as follows:

items.text: Capsular ligament (joint capsule).
Iliofemoral ligament (strongest).
Pubofemoral ligament.
Ischiofemoral ligament.
Transverse acetabular ligament.
Acetabular labrum.
Ligamentum teres femoris (round ligament of the head of femur).

blocks.text: 1. The capsular ligament is a strong and dense fibrous sac which encloses the joint.

The capsule is made up of two types of fibres—inner circular fibres and outer longitudinal fibres. The inner circular fibres form a collar around the femoral neck (zona orbicularis). These fibres are not directly attached to the bones (Statement 1) The outer longitudinal fibres are reflected along the neck toward the head to form the retinacula.

2. The iliofemoral ligament is an inverted Y-shaped ligament, which lies anteriorly and intimately blended with the capsule.(Statement 3) This ligament consists of three parts: a lateral thick band of oblique fibres,a medial thick band of vertical fibres, and a large central thin portion Iliofemoral ligament is the strongest ligament of body and prevents the trunk from falling backward in the standing posture
3. The pubofemoral ligament is a triangular ligament with base above and apex below
4. The ischiofemoral ligament is relatively weak and supports the capsule posteriorly
5. Round ligament of head of femur: This ligament is also called ligamentum teres of the head of the femur.

It is a flat triangular ligament with apex attached to the fovea of the head, and its base to the transverse acetabular ligament It is ensheathed by a conical reflection of the synovial membrane. It does not increase the stability of the joint.

It transmits arteries to the head of the femur derived from the acetabular branches of the obturator and medial circumflex femoral arteries.(Statement 2) Morphologically, the ligament of the head of femur represents the part of capsule that has been included within the joint
6. The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the acetabular margin.
The labrum not only deepens the acetabulum (socket) but grasps the head of femur lightly to hold it in position.(Statement 4)

7. Transverse acetabular ligament: It is a part of acetabular labrum, which bridges the acetabular notch; however, it is devoid of cartilage cells. The acetabular notch thus becomes converted into the foramen which transmits the acetabular vessels and nerves to the hip joint.

Prepatalar bursitis also known as Housemaid’s knee is the inflammation of the prepatellar bursa (prepatellar bursitis). It occurs due to friction of bursa against the patella when it comes in contact with the ground during scrubbing of the floor by the housemaid. Such a bursa may get very large and drop by its weight too much below to its original position. Subcutaneous prepatellar bursa (bursa of housemaid’s knee).
It lies deep to the skin in front of the lower half of the patella and upper half of the ligamentum patellae and tibial tuberosity.
**Baker’s cyst (Option B):** The chronic inflammation of bursa deep to semimembranosus may present as cystic swelling in the medial part of the popliteal fossa called Baker’s cyst

**Osteoarthritis of the knee (Option C):** This is unlikely given the patient's relatively young age and the acute nature of the symptoms. Osteoarthritis typically presents with chronic pain, stiffness, and decreased range of motion in older individuals, especially those over the age of 50. The swelling in osteoarthritis is also typically associated with joint degeneration rather than soft, fluctuant swelling in the prepatellar region.

**Clergyman’s knee (Option D):** It is the inflammation of subcutaneous infrapatellar bursa (subcutaneous infrapatellar bursitis). It occurs due to the friction of bursa against the tibial tuberosity due to kneeling (e.g., kneeling during prayer by Christian priests/clergymen, roofers, and floor tilers.

The patient’s symptoms, including weakness in hip extension, knee flexion, and sensory loss along the posterior thigh and leg, are indicative of sciatic nerve injury.
The sciatic nerve originates from the ventral rami of the L4–S3 spinal roots.
**Sciatic Nerve Origin and Course:** The thickest nerve in the body.

items.text: Arises from the ventral rami of L4–S3 spinal nerves. (Option A, C & D ruled out)
Exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis and descends between the greater trochanter and ischial tuberosity along the back of the thigh.
Divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves above the popliteal fossa.

blocks.text: Distribution
**Motor:**

items.text: **Undivided Trunk:** Supplies all muscles of the back of the thigh (hip extension, knee flexion).
**Tibial Nerve:** Innervates leg muscles (flexion) and foot muscles (plantar flexion).
**Common Peroneal Nerve:** Supplies leg muscles (dorsiflexion).

blocks.text: **Sensory:**

items.text: **Tibial Nerve:** Supplies skin on the back of the calf, heel, lateral border of the foot, and sole.
**Common Peroneal Nerve:** Supplies skin on the anterolateral and lateral surfaces of the leg and dorsum of the foot (except for the deep peroneal nerve area).

blocks.text: Clinical correlation
**Injury of the sciatic nerve:**
**Causes:** Penetrating wounds, posterior hip dislocation, pelvic fractures, total hip replacement, misplaced injections in the gluteal region.
**Clinical Features:**

items.text: Inability to extend the thigh and flex the knee (hamstring paralysis).
Loss of all movements below the knee (foot drop) leading to flail foot and high-stepping gait.
Loss of sensation on the back of the thigh, entire leg, and foot (except for the saphenous nerve area).

blocks.text: Sciatica: Shooting pain along the sciatic nerve distribution (buttock, posterior thigh, lateral leg, dorsum of the foot). Compression/irritation of L4–S3 spinal nerve roots due to herniated lumbar discs.

The popliteus muscle originates from the anterior part of the popliteal groove on the lateral condyle of the femur and is supplied by a branch of the tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1).
Popliteus Muscle
**Popliteus Muscle**
**Origin:** Arises within the knee joint capsule from the anterior part of the popliteal groove located on the lateral condyle of the femur.
**Insertion:** The medial aspect of the head of the fibula via the popliteofibular ligament Medial two-thirds of the triangular area above the soleal line on the posterior surface of the tibia.
**Blood supply:** Inferior medial and lateral genicular arteries Posterior tibial artery and its branches.
**Nerve supply:** The branch of the tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1).
**Actions:** Medially rotates the tibia on the femur; when the tibia is fixed, it laterally rotates the femur.

It is the "unlocking" muscle of the knee by unlocking the locked knee by rotating the femur laterally during the initial stages of knee flexion. It pulls the lateral meniscus posteriorly, preventing it from becoming trapped and compressed between the femoral and tibial condyles.

Options A, C, and D are incorrect because the popliteus muscle originates from the lateral condyle of the femur, not the medial condyle, the tibial tuberosity or the fibular head, respectively, and it is innervated by the tibial nerve, not the femoral nerve, sciatic nerve, or peroneal nerve respectively.

The common peroneal nerve runs obliquely through the lateral aspect of the popliteal fossa, and injury or compression can lead to weakness in dorsiflexion (foot drop) and sensory loss over the lateral leg.
Contents of the Popliteal Fossa:

items.text: **Popliteal artery:** Deepest structure, crossed posteriorly by the popliteal vein and tibial nerve.
**Popliteal vein:** Located anterior to the tibial nerve, crosses the artery.
**Tibial nerve:** Most superficial, runs vertically and crosses the fossa.
**Common peroneal nerve:** Runs obliquely from the superior to the lateral angle of the fossa.
The posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh is located in the popliteal fossa.
**Genicular branch of the obturator nerve:** Follows the popliteal artery to the knee.
**Popliteal lymph nodes:** 6-7 nodes embedded in fat.
**Fat:** Surrounds and supports all the structures.

blocks.text: Relations:

items.text: **In the middle part of the fossa, Superficial to deep:** Tibial nerve → Popliteal vein → Popliteal artery (NVA)
**In the upper part of the fossa, Lateral to Medial:** Tibial nerve → Popliteal vein → Popliteal artery (NVA)
**In the lower part of the fossa, Lateral to Medial:** Popliteal artery → Popliteal vein → Tibial Nerve (AVN)

**Ligamentum Patellae:** Attaches from the lower border of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. Continuation of the quadriceps femoris tendon.

**Lateral (Fibular) Collateral Ligament:** (Option B ruled out) Cord-like structure attaching from the femur's lateral condyle to the fibula's head. The Popliteus tendon is located between this ligament and the lateral meniscus.
**Medial (Tibial) Collateral Ligament:** Flat band connecting the medial condyle of the femur to the medial surface of the tibia. Firmly attached to the medial meniscus.
**Oblique Popliteal Ligament:** Tendinous expansion from the semimembranosus muscle, strengthening the posterior capsule.

**Medial Meniscus:** Semicircular, wider posteriorly than anteriorly. (Option C ruled out) The peripheral margin adheres to the deep part of the tibial collateral ligament; posterior fibres are continuous with the transverse ligament.

**Lateral Meniscus:** Circular. The posterior end is attached to the medial condyle of the femur via two meniscofemoral ligaments; separated from the fibular collateral ligament by the popliteus tendon.
**Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL):** (Option A ruled out) It attaches to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia and ascends to the posterior part of the lateral femoral condyle.
Prevents posterior displacement of the femur and anterior displacement of the tibia when the knee is flexed. It is extrasynovial.

**Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL):** It attaches to the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia and extends to the anterior part of the medial femoral condyle. Prevents anterior displacement of the femur and posterior displacement of the tibia when the knee is flexed. It is extrasynovial.

**Classification of Ligaments and Menisci by Location and Synovial Relation:**

items.text: **Intracapsular and Intrasynovial:** Menisci (lie within the joint capsule and are bathed by synovial fluid).
**Intracapsular but Extrasynovial:** Cruciate ligaments (located within the joint capsule but outside the synovial cavity).
**Extracapsular and Extrasynovial:** Collateral ligaments (outside both the joint capsule and synovial cavity).

blocks.text: The quadriceps femoris muscle group extends the knee and helps in the locking mechanism when the knee is fully extended. The popliteus muscle is responsible for unlocking the knee by initiating flexion, particularly from a fully extended position.

blocks.text: **Locking and Unlocking Mechanism of the Knee (Non-Weight-Bearing)**
**Locking (Screw-Home Mechanism):** During knee extension, the tibia medially rotates relative to the femur, tightening ligaments (e.g., ACL) and stabilising the joint.
**Unlocking:** The popliteus muscle initiates knee flexion by laterally rotating the tibia, loosening the ligaments and allowing movement.
This mechanism ensures stability during transitions and controlled movement when the foot is not planted.
